name: three-rs
title: More Than Tokens: The Three R’s
kicker: What the business needs · and what everyone’s excited about
html:
More Than Tokens: The Three R’s

Only what the state allows. When an act is absent, a reason.

That right behavior, the same way, every time.

The server changes, or misbehaves. The client takes the right failure path and carries on.

is the hype. A reasoning model can stand in for a person in two places: finding the way the first time, and repairing when the controls change. In the middle, it’s the token maxing Hightower warned us about.

Repeatable: given the same inputs, the same outputs, call after call. All three together are what people mean by ; miss one and it’s gone.

Every part of this talk gets measured against these three.
say: Ask anyone who runs a business process what they need from an agent, and I doubt they'll say 'more reasoning'. They need three R's, in this order. Right behavior first: the agent only does what the current state allows, and when it can't, it gets told why. Then repeatability: given the same inputs, the same outputs, call after call. Then resilience: when the server changes, or misbehaves, the agent takes the failure path it's supposed to and carries on. And reason? Reason is the hype. It's what everyone's excited about when they talk about agents. Reasoning models really can stand in for a person, in two places: finding the way the first time, and repairing when the controls change. In the middle, paying a model to reason through the same path again is the token maxing Hightower warned us about. Get all three and you have something people can rely on. Miss one and you don't. Keep these pills in mind; every part of this talk gets measured against these three. And what are they for? Ask anyone in insurance.

deck:ref.name: right-behavior
deck:ref.label: RIGHT-BEHAVIOR
deck:ref.title: Right behavior: only what the state allows, and a reason when not
deck:ref.summary: The agent is offered only the acts the current state allows, sends each one with the validator from the state it read, and gets a reason when an act is absent. At the small scale it is a Gherkin scenario that says what right means before any code is written.

deck:ref.name: repeatability
deck:ref.label: REPEATABILITY
deck:ref.title: Repeatability: the same goal, the same result, every time
deck:ref.summary: Given the same inputs, the same outputs, call after call. Found once with a model, then replayed with none: the same steps, the same checks, the same result, until the controls really change. At the small scale it is one scenario that runs the same way every time.
deck:ref.cite: The second of the three R's

describedby.title: The second of the three R's

deck:ref.name: resilience
deck:ref.label: RESILIENCE
deck:ref.title: Resilience: the server changes, the client doesn't break
deck:ref.summary: When the server changes, or misbehaves on purpose, the client takes the failure path the spec names, re-syncs, and goes on; a model comes back only when the controls really changed, to repair. At the small scale it is the regression suite and the gates that hold, even against the model.

deck:ref.label: REASON
deck:ref.title: Reason: the part everyone's excited about
deck:ref.summary: Reasoning models can stand in for a person in two places: finding the way the first time, and repairing when the controls change. Everywhere else, paying a model to reason through the same path again is the token maxing Hightower warned about. Useful at the edges; wasted in the middle.

deck:ref.name: reliability
deck:ref.label: RELIABILITY
deck:ref.title: Reliability: what the three R's add up to
deck:ref.summary: Not a fourth R beside the others: the one over them. A system is reliable only when it behaves right, repeats that behavior given the same inputs, and stays right when things change or break. Miss any one and it isn't.
